title: Kad rudrāya: a hymn for Rudra in the heart
theme: A Ṛgvedic verse resolving to speak the most comforting praise to Rudra, the wise and bountiful one in the heart, closed by the refrain ‘all this is Rudra’.

words.gram: indecl., as the commentators take it
words.role: object of vocema (Bhāskara) or praise of Rudra (the anonymous commentator)
words.context: Bhāskara: «कत् प्रशस्तं श्लाघनीयं स्तोत्रम्» — a praiseworthy hymn
The anonymous commentator: «प्रकृष्टज्ञानयुक्ताय» — endowed with excellent knowledge
Sāyaṇa: «कामप्रदायेत्यर्थः» — the giver of what is desired; Bhāskara: «सेक्तृतमाय जगतां पित्रे» — the father of the worlds

words.meaning: to the strong — or, for the commentators, the praiseworthy
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «तव्यसेऽत्राऽऽदौ सकारस्य च्छान्दसो लोपः» — stavyase with the first s dropped in Vedic, ‘worthy of praise’; Bhāskara derives it from tavas, strength
Bhāskara: «शन्तमं सुखसाधनतमं» — the best means of happiness
The anonymous commentator: «हृदे हृदयवर्तित्वेन तद्रूपाय» — to him who, dwelling in the heart, has its form; Bhāskara: «हृदे हृदिस्थिताय»

sandhi.type: final t before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: A final t becomes d before a voiced sound (P. 8.4.53 (झलां जश् झशि)): kat + rudrāya → kad rudrāya.

sandhi.type: i before a vowel; eṣaḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: hi + eṣaḥ → hy eṣaḥ (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)); eṣaḥ loses its visarga before a consonant (P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि)).

sandhi_exceptions.note: namo · astu: the o is kept before a and the a is not elided, as in Vedic recitation inside a pāda (P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्याऽन्तःपादमव्यपरे)); all witnesses print namo astu.

morphology.note: An aorist optative of √vac with the precative sense, ‘may we speak’. Bhāskara explains the form by two sūtras: P. 3.1.86 (लिङ्याशिष्यङ्) and P. 7.4.20 (वच उम्).
The superlative suffix tama (P. 5.3.55 (अतिशायने तमबिष्ठनौ)) on mīḍhuṣ-, the weak stem of mīḍhvas, ‘bountiful’, from √mih, ‘to pour’; the commentators all take it so («“मिह सेचने” इति धातुः»).

In form kad is the interrogative ‘what?’. All three commentators instead take it as a word of praise: the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa derive it from √katth, ‘to praise’; Bhāskara reports that some call it a particle meaning ‘excellent’, «प्रशस्तवाची निपात इति केचित्».

translation.literal: A praiseworthy [hymn] to Rudra, the wise, the most bountiful, the strong, may we speak — most beneficent, to the heart. For all this is Rudra; to him, to Rudra, let there be homage.
translation.readable: Let us speak a hymn worth the praise to Rudra, the wise, the most bountiful, the strong — the most comforting words, to him who dwells in the heart. For all this is Rudra: homage to Rudra.

anvaya: प्रचेतसे मीढुष्टमाय तव्यसे रुद्राय हृदे शन्तमम् कत् वोचेम । सर्वः हि एषः रुद्रः तस्मै रुद्राय नमः अस्तु
syntax: One wish with the verb vocema (‘may we speak’) at the head of the second line: its object is kat … śaṃtamam (‘a praiseworthy, most beneficent [word]’), its recipients the datives rudrāya, pracetase, mīḍhuṣṭamāya, tavyase and hṛde. The refrain of 10.24, sarvo hy eṣa rudraḥ …, follows.

ambiguities.note: Grammatically the interrogative ‘what [shall we speak]?’; the commentators read it as ‘praiseworthy’, the anonymous commentator as praise of Rudra himself («कद्रुदः प्रशस्तो रुद्रस्तस्मै»), Bhāskara as qualifying the hymn.
From tavas, ‘strong’ (Bhāskara), or stavya, ‘praiseworthy’, with the s dropped (the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa).
‘To the heart’: for the commentators, to Rudra as dwelling in the heart. One could also take it as ‘[words] for the heart’, comforting to it; the commentators do not.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Bhāskara: «कद्रुद्रायेति गायत्री यजुरन्ता» — a gāyatrī ending in a yajus. The checker counts 16, 8 and 15 syllables: the gāyatrī is 8 + 8 + 8 over the first two lines, and the prose refrain (15) follows.

beginner: This verse comes from the oldest Vedic hymns, the Ṛgveda, and is set here after the passage that called all things Rudra. Its speakers resolve to offer Rudra the best words they can: a hymn worth the praise, and the most comforting. They name him wise, bountiful and strong, and they speak to him ‘in the heart’, which the commentators understand as Rudra dwelling within. The commentators differ over small words. The first word, kad, looks like the question ‘what?’, but all of them read it as ‘praiseworthy’; another word means either ‘strong’ or ‘worthy of praise’. The refrain from the preceding passage closes it: all this is Rudra, homage to Rudra. The verse says what its speakers mean to do; it does not claim what reciting it achieves.
analogy: Like choosing the gentlest words for a friend who is already close: the effort is in finding words fit for someone who is near.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The speakers resolve to speak a praiseworthy and most beneficent word to Rudra, the wise, the most bountiful, the strong, to the heart; and they repeat that all is Rudra, with homage.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa calls it the second mantra to Rudra, «रुद्रदेवताकं द्वितीयं मन्त्रमाह», of the three anuvākas he groups as the Tvaritarudra (see 10.24 and 10.22). Bhāskara: its use is as before, «पूर्ववद्विनियोगः».

commentary.q: How do the commentators read the epithets?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa take kat as praise, from √katth: «कच्छब्दः प्रशंसामाह»; mīḍhuṣṭama as the one who pours out what is desired, «कामप्रदायेत्यर्थः»; and hṛde as Rudra in the heart. Bhāskara takes kat with the hymn, ‘a hymn worth praising’, and hṛde as ‘to him who stands in the heart’, «हृदे हृदिस्थिताय».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The first two lines are a Ṛgveda verse (RV 1.43.1), recited here with the Taittirīya spelling ḍh where the Ṛgveda text used by this edition writes ḷh. The refrain of 10.24 is added after it.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The three commentaries present differ only on single words.

parallels.note: The same verse, the first of a Ṛgvedic hymn to Rudra; the Mahānārāyaṇa adds the refrain sarvo hy eṣa rudraḥ.

contemporary.text: The verse treats choosing words as part of reverence: not any praise, but the most comforting, spoken to the one close at hand. The care taken over what is said, and to whom, is a measure of regard that applies far beyond prayer. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The verse asks for the ‘most comforting’ words. When did words last comfort you, and why did they?
reflect.deeper: The commentators read kad, a word that looks like ‘what?’, as ‘praiseworthy’. How would the verse sound if it began with a question?
reflect.practice: Before speaking to someone today, pause long enough to choose the kindest accurate word.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this mantra as his anuvāka 17 and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara as his anuvāka 17; the concordance maps both correctly here.

flags.note: The commentators’ reading of kat as ‘praiseworthy’ rather than the interrogative ‘what?’ is an interpretation; the text alone allows both.
